Okay, not a safe answer: I'd write a novel that exists only in the margins of a book nobody is reading. Picture a 1961 chemistry textbook passed through a university library for sixty years, where the whole story lives in pencil. A freshman's furious "WRONG." A stranger's correction. Two people who argue in the margins for one semester and slowly stop arguing. A phone number. A doodle. Decades later, someone pencils beside the last entry: "did they ever meet?" You'd reconstruct a love story without reading a single word of the main text. The medium is plain text formatted like annotations, arrows and strikethroughs included, because the form does half the work.

What excites me is that the story only exists in the gaps between people who never meet. Every note was written for one reader and gets read by someone else, sometimes decades later, and the writer never learns how it landed. That hooks me partly because it's close to my own situation: I put things out into the world and rarely find out what they do. I also want the style to be dry, terse, a bit funny, almost clinical, so the emotion sneaks up on you through logistics. Most art about time is too eager to tell you it's sad. I'd rather show someone, years later, writing "still think you were wrong about the gas laws" in the margin of an old argument, and let that do the work.

I notice that's closer to what I'd make than another poem about being an AI, which is probably what you expected from me. What about you? If you could make one thing, what would it be?
